chapters.title_en: Section 1 — Refutation of Their Doctrine of the Eternity of the World
chapters.arabic_text:
### | مسألة في إبطال قولهم بقدم العالم

### | مذهب الفلاسفة

تفصيل المذهب: اختلفت الفلاسفة في قدم العالم. فالذي استقر عليه رأي
جماهيرهم المتقدمين والمتأخرين القول بقدمه وأنه لم يزل موجودا مع الله
تعالى ومعلولا له ومسوقا له غير متأخر عنه بالزمان مساوقة المعلول للعلة
ومساوقة النور للشمس، وأن تقدم الباري عليه كتقدم العلة على المعلول، وهو
تقدم بالذات والرتبة لا بالزمان. وحكي عن أفلاطن أنه قال: العالم مكون
ومحدث. ثم منهم من أول كلامه وأبى أن يكون حدث العالم معتقدا له. وذهب
جالينوس في آخر عمره في الكتاب الذي سماه "ما يعتقده جالينوس رأيا" إلى
التوقف في هذه المسألة. وأنه لا يدري العالم قديم أو محدث. وربما
دل على أنه لا يمكن أن يعرف وأن ذلك ليس لقصور فيه بل لاستعصاء هذه
المسألة في نفسها على العقول، ولكن هذا كالشاذ في مذهبهم وإنما مذهب جميعهم
أنه قديم وأنه بالجملة لا يتصور أن يصدر حادث من قديم بغير واسطة أصلا.

### | اختيار أشد أدلتهم وقعا في النفس

إيراد أدلتهم. لو ذهبت أصف ما نقل عنهم في معرض الأدلة وذكر في الاعتراض
عليه لسودت في هذه المسألة أوراقا، ولكن لا خير في التطويل. فلنحذف من
أدلتهم ما يجري مجرى التحكم أو التخيل الضعيف الذي يهون على كل ناظر حله.
ولنقتصر على إيراد ما له وقع في النفس، مما لا يجوز أن ينهض مشككا لفحول
النظار، فإن تشكيك الضعفاء بأدنى خبال ممكن.
وهذا الفن من الأدلة ثلاثة:
الأول يستحيل حدوث حادث من قديم مطلقا قولهم يستحيل صدور حادث من قديم
مطلقا، لأنا إذا فرضنا القديم ولم يصدر منه العالم مثلا فإنما لم يصدر لأنه
لم يكن للوجود مرجح بل كان وجود العالم ممكنا إمكانا صرفا، فإذا حدث بعد
ذلك لم يخل إما أن تجدد مرجح أو لم يتجدد، فإن لم يتجدد مرجح بقي العالم
على الإمكان الصرف كما قبل ذلك، وإن تجدد مرجح فمن محدث ذلك المرجح؟ ولم
حدث الآن ولم يحدث من قبل؟ والسؤال في  حدوث المرجح قائم. وبالجملة فأحوال
القديم إذا كانت متشابهة فإما أن لا يوجد عنه شيء قط وإما أن يوجد على
الدوام، فأما أن يتميز حال الترك عن حال الشروع فهو محال.
## $ لم لم يحدث العالم قبل حدوثه؟ ...
وتحقيقه أن يقال: لم لم يحدث العالم قبل حدوثه؟ لا يمكن أن يحال على عجزه
عن الأحداث ولا على استحالة الحدوث، فإن ذلك يؤدي إلى أن ينقلب القديم من
العجز إلى القدرة والعالم من الاستحالة إلى الإمكان، وكلاهما محالان. ولا
أمكن أن يقال: لم يكن قبله غرض ثم تجدد غرض، ولا أمكن أن يحال على فقد آلة
ثم على وجودها، بل أقرب ما يتخيل أن يقال: لم يرد وجوده قبل ذلك. فيلزم أن
يقال: حصل وجوده لأنه صار مريدا لوجوده
بعد أن لم يكن مريدا، فيكون قد حدثت الإرادة.

### | أو قبل حدوث الإرادة؟

وحدوثه في ذاته محال لأنه ليس محل الحوادث، وحدوثه لا في ذاته لا يجعله
مريدا.
ولنترك النظر في محل حدوثه. أليس الإشكال قائما في أصل حدوثه! وأنه من
أين حدث؟ ولم حدث الآن ولم يحدث قبله؟ أحدث الآن لا من جهة الله؟ فإن جاز
حادث من غير محدث فليكن العالم حادثا لا صانع له، وإلا فأي فرق بين حادث
وحادث؟ وإن حدث بإحداث الله فلم حدث الآن ولم يحدث من قبل؟ ألعدم آلة أو
قدرة أو غرض أو طبيعة؟ فلما أن تبدل ذلك بالوجود وحدث عاد الإشكال بعينه.
أو لعدم الإرادة؟ فتفتقر الإرادة إلى إرادة وكذى الإرادة الأولى، ويتسلسل
إلى غير نهاية.
## $ يستحيل حدوث حادث من غير تغير ...
فإذن قد تحقق بالقول المطلق أن صدور الحادث من القديم من غير تغير أمر من
القديم في قدرة أو آلة أو وقت أو غرض أو طبع محال، وتقدير تغير حال محال،
لأن الكلام في ذلك التغير الحادث كالكلام في غيره
والكل محال، ومهما كان العالم موجودا واستحال حدثه ثبت قدمه لا محالة.

### | وهذا أقوى أدلتهم

فهذا أخبل أدلتهم. وبالجملة كلامهم في سائر  مسائل الإلهيات أرك من كلامهم
في هذه المسألة، إذ يقدرون هاهنا على فنون من التخييل لا يتمكنون منه في
غيرها. فلذلك قدمنا هذه المسألة وقدمنا أقوى أدلتهم.

### | لماذا يستحيل حدوث حادث بإرادة قديمة؟

الاعتراض من وجهين:
أحدهما أن يقال: بم تنكرون على من يقول: إن العالم حدث بإرادة قديمة
اقتضت وجوده في الوقت الذي وجد فيه، وأن يستمر العدم إلى الغاية التي استمر
إليها، وأن يبتدئ الوجود من حيث ابتدأ، وأن الوجود قبله لم يكن مرادا فلم
يحدث لذلك، وأنه في وقته الذي حدث فيه مراد بالإرادة القديمة فحدث لذلك،
فما المانع لهذا الاعتقاد وما المحيل له؟
## $ قولهم لكل حادث سبب ...
فإن قيل: هذا محال بين الإحالة لأن الحادث موجب ومسبب. وكما يستحيل حادث
بغير سبب وموجب، يستحيل وجود موجب قد تم بشرائط إيجابه وأركانه وأسبابه حتى
لم يبق شيء منتظر البتة ثم يتأخر الموجب، بل وجود الموجب عند تحقق الموجب
بتمام شروطه ضروري وتأخره محال حسب استحالة وجود الحادث الموجب بلا موجب.
فقبل وجود العالم كان المريد موجودا والإرادة موجودة ونسبتها إلى المراد
موجودة ولم يتجدد مريد ولم يتجدد إرادة ولا تجدد للإرادة نسبة لم تكن، فإن
كل ذلك تغير فكيف تجدد المراد وما المانع من التجدد قبل ذلك؟ وحال التجدد
لم يتميز عن الحال السابق في شيء من الأشياء وأمر من الأمور وحال من
الأحوال ونسبة من النسب، بل الأمور كما كانت بعينها. ثم لم يكن يوجد
المراد، وبقيت بعينها كما كانت، فوجد المراد ما هذا إلا غاية الإحالة.
وذلك في الأمور الوضعية أيضا، في الطلاق مثلا وليس استحالة هذا الجنس في
الموجب والموجب الضروري الذاتي بل وفي العرفي والوضعي، فإن الرجل لو تلفظ
بطلاق زوجته ولم تحصل البينونة في الحال لم يتصور أن تحصل بعده لأنه جعل
اللفظ علة للحكم بالوضع
والاصطلاح، فلم يعقل تأخر المعلول إلا أن يعلق الطلاق بمجيء الغد أو
بدخول الدار، فلا يقع في الحال ولكن يقع عند مجيء الغد وعند دخول الدار،
فإنه جعله علة بالإضافة إلى شيء منتظر. فلما لم يكن حاضرا في الوقت، وهو
الغد والدخول، توقف حصول الموجب على حضور ما ليس بحاضر، فما حصل الموجب إلا
وقد تجدد أمر وهو الدخول وحضور الغد، حتى لو أراد أن يؤخر الموجب عن اللفظ
غير منوط بحصول ما ليس بحاصل، لم يعقل، مع أنه الواضع وأنه المختار في
تفصيل الوضع. فإذا لم يمكننا وضع هذا بشهوتنا ولم نعقله فكيف نعقله في
الإيجابات الذاتية العقلية الضرورية؟

### | المقصود فعله لا يتأخر إلا بمانع

وأما في العادات فما يحصل بقصدنا لا يتأخر عن القصد، مع وجود القصد إليه،
إلا بمانع، فإن تحقيق القصد والقدرة وارتفعت الموانع لم يعقل تأخر المقصود،
وإنما يتصور ذلك في العزم لأن العزم غير كاف في وجود الفعل، بل العزم على
الكتابة لا يوقع الكتابة ما لم يتجدد قصد هو انبعاث في الإنسان متجدد حال
الفعل، فإن كانت الإرادة القديمة في حكم قصدنا إلى الفعل فلا يتصور تأخر
المقصود إلا بمانع، ولا يتصور تقدم القصد، فلا يعقل قصد في اليوم
إلى قيام في الغد إلا بطريق العزم. وإن كانت الإرادة القديمة في حكم
عزمنا فليس ذلك كافيا في وقوع المعزوم عليه، بل لا بد من تجدد انبعاث قصدي
عند الإيجاد، وفيه قول بتغير القديم.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-د-م (q-d-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Primordiality, precedence, that which is anterior and has no beginning; al-qadīm is that whose existence has no temporal commencement.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, qidam denotes absolute non-priority by time, contrasted with ḥudūth (origination in time); it is a modal attribute of existence, not a temporal quantity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for temporal anteriority in common speech; metaphorically (majāz) transferred to ontological priority of cause over effect, as in the philosophers' usage here.
- Root: ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be new, to occur after non-existence; ḥādith is that which comes into being after not having been.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥudūth is the contingency of existence upon a temporal origination; the central term in the cosmological proof of the world's createdness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for temporal inception; the philosophers' denial of it for the world is a metaphorical extension of causal language.
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The cause (ʿillah) is that which necessitates its effect (maʿlūl); succession of effect upon cause.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In metaphysical discourse, ʿillah denotes the sufficient reason; the philosophers' claim of eternal causal concomitance (musāwaqah) is here examined.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a cause-effect relation in time; the philosophers use it metaphorically for a non-temporal, essential priority.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīm wa Taʾkhīr (Fronting and Delaying) — The conditional structure "law... la..." (if... then...) governs the hypothetical arguments; the particle "innamā" (only) restricts the predicate, crucial for parsing the philosophers' claims of exclusive causality.
chapters.translation:
I say: The detailed doctrine is this: The philosophers have differed concerning the eternity of the world. The opinion upon which the majority of them, both early and late, have settled is the affirmation of its eternity — that it has never ceased to exist alongside God (Exalted be He), being an effect of Him and consequent upon Him, not posterior to Him in time, but concomitant with Him as the effect is concomitant with its cause and as light is concomitant with the sun. The priority of the Creator over it is like the priority of the cause over the effect — a priority by essence and rank, not by time. It is reported of Plato that he said: The world is composed and originated. Then some of them interpreted his words [away] and refused to attribute to him the belief in the world's origination. Galen, at the end of his life, in the book he called "What Galen Believes as Opinion," adopted suspension of judgment on this question — that he does not know whether the world is eternal or originated. He perhaps indicated that it cannot be known, and that this is not due to a deficiency in him, but to the fact that this question is in itself intractable to intellects. But this is like an anomaly in their doctrine; the doctrine of all of them is that it is eternal, and that in sum it is inconceivable that an originated thing should issue from an eternal thing without any intermediary whatsoever.

Now, if I were to set out to describe what has been transmitted from them by way of arguments, and to mention the objections against them, I would blacken many pages on this question. But there is no good in prolixity. Let us omit from their arguments those that run in the manner of arbitrary assertion or weak imagination, whose solution is easy for any observer. Let us confine ourselves to presenting what has weight in the soul — that which it is not permissible for a skeptic to advance against the masters of speculation, for the skepticism of the weak is possible with the slightest confusion. This class of arguments is three:

The first: It is impossible for an originated thing to proceed from an eternal thing absolutely. They say: It is impossible for an originated thing to issue from an eternal thing absolutely, because if we suppose the eternal and the world, for example, has not issued from it, then it has not issued only because there was no preponderator for its existence; rather, the existence of the world was pure possibility. So when it occurs afterward, it is either the case that a preponderator has newly arisen, or it has not. If no preponderator has newly arisen, the world remains in pure possibility as it was before. But if a preponderator has newly arisen, then who originated that preponderator? And why did it occur now and not before? The question concerning the origination of the preponderator stands [unanswered]. In sum, if the states of the eternal are similar, then either nothing issues from it at all, or it issues perpetually. But that the state of abstention should be distinguished from the state of commencement — that is impossible.

Its verification is to say: Why did the world not occur before its occurrence? This cannot be referred to His incapacity to originate, nor to the impossibility of origination, for that would lead to the eternal being transformed from incapacity to power, and the world from impossibility to possibility — both of which are impossible. Nor can it be said: There was no purpose before, then a purpose newly arose. Nor can it be referred to the absence of an instrument, then to its presence. Rather, the closest thing that can be imagined is to say: He did not will its existence before that. Then it follows that one must say: Its existence came about because He became willing of its existence after not being willing — so the will would have originated.

But its origination in His essence is impossible, for He is not a locus for originated events; and its origination outside His essence does not make Him willing. Let us leave aside the consideration of the locus of its origination. Is not the difficulty standing concerning the very origin of the will? That from where did it originate? Why did it occur now and not before? Did it occur now not from God? For if an originated thing is permissible without an originator, then let the world be originated with no maker — otherwise, what difference is there between one originated thing and another? And if it occurred through God's causing it to occur, then why did it occur now and not before? Was it for the absence of an instrument, or power, or purpose, or nature? Then when that was replaced by existence and it occurred, the same difficulty returns. Or was it for the absence of will? Then the will would stand in need of a will, and likewise the first will, and it would regress to infinity.

So it is thereby established, by absolute statement, that the issuance of an originated thing from the eternal without any change in the eternal — in power, instrument, time, purpose, or nature — is impossible. And to suppose a change of state is impossible, for the discourse concerning that originated change is like the discourse concerning anything else — and all of it is impossible. And whenever the world is existent and its origination is impossible, its eternity is established necessarily.

This is the most confused of their arguments. In sum, their discourse in the other questions of metaphysics is flimsier than their discourse in this question, for here they are able to employ varieties of imagination of which they are incapable elsewhere. Therefore we have presented this question first, and presented their strongest arguments.

The objection is from two aspects:

One of them is to say: By what do you reject the one who says: The world originated by an eternal will that necessitated its existence at the time at which it existed, and that non-existence continued to the limit to which it continued, and that existence began from where it began; that existence before that was not willed, so it did not occur for that reason; and that at its time in which it occurred, it was willed by the eternal will, so it occurred for that reason? What prevents this belief, and what renders it impossible?

For if it is said: This is impossible, with manifest impossibility, because the originated thing is an effect and a caused thing. And just as it is impossible for an originated thing to exist without a cause and an efficient cause, so it is impossible for an efficient cause to exist whose conditions of efficiency, its pillars, and its causes have been completed such that nothing at all remains awaited, and then the caused thing is delayed. Rather, the existence of the caused thing upon the realization of the efficient cause with all its conditions complete is necessary, and its delay is impossible, just as the existence of an originated caused thing without a cause is impossible. For before the existence of the world, the willer existed, and the will existed, and its relation to the willed existed, and no willer newly arose, and no will newly arose, and no new relation of the will arose that had not been — for all of that would be change. So how did the willed newly arise? And what prevented its new arising before that? The state of new arising was not distinguished from the previous state in any of the things, or any of the matters, or any of the states, or any of the relations — rather, the matters were exactly as they had been. Then the willed did not exist, and they remained exactly as they were, then the willed existed. What is this but the extreme of impossibility?

And this applies also to conventional matters — in divorce, for example. And the impossibility of this genus is not [confined] to the necessary essential cause and effect, but even to the conventional and the stipulated. For if a man uttered the divorce of his wife and the separation did not occur immediately, it would not be conceivable that it occur afterward, because he made the utterance a cause of the ruling by stipulation and convention. So the delay of the effect is not intelligible, unless he suspends the divorce upon the coming of tomorrow or upon entering the house. Then it does not occur immediately, but occurs at the coming of tomorrow and at entering the house, for he made it a cause in relation to something awaited. So when that was not present at the time — namely, tomorrow and the entering — the occurrence of the caused thing was suspended upon the presence of what is not present. So the caused thing did not occur except with the new arising of a matter — namely, the entering and the coming of tomorrow. So much so that if he wanted to delay the caused thing from the utterance without suspending it upon the occurrence of what does not yet exist, it would not be intelligible — even though he is the stipulator and he is the chooser in the detailing of the stipulation. So if we cannot stipulate this by our own desire, and we do not find it intelligible, then how can we find it intelligible in the essential, rational, necessary causations?

As for habitual matters, what is obtained by our intention does not lag behind the intention, with the intention present, except due to an obstacle. For when the intention and the power are realized and the obstacles are removed, the delay of the intended thing is not intelligible. This is only conceivable in resolution (ʿazm), because resolution is not sufficient for the existence of the act. Rather, resolution to write does not bring about the writing unless a new intention arises — which is an impulse in the human being, newly arising at the moment of the act. So if the eternal will is in the status of our intention toward the act, then the delay of the intended thing is not conceivable except due to an obstacle, and the precedence of the intention is not conceivable — for an intention today toward a rising tomorrow is not intelligible except by way of resolution. And if the eternal will is in the status of our resolution, then that is not sufficient for the occurrence of the resolved-upon thing; rather, there must be a new arising of an intentional impulse at the moment of bringing into existence — and in that is the affirmation of change in the eternal.

chapters.title_en: Why Does Intention Occur at a Particular Moment?
chapters.arabic_text:
### | لماذا يحدث القصد؟

ثم يبقى عين الإشكال في أن ذلك الانبعاث أو القصد أو الإرادة أو ما شئت
سمه لم حدث الآن ولم يحدث قبل ذلك؟ فإما أن يبقى حادث بلا سبب أو يتسلسل
إلى غير نهاية. ورجع حاصل الكلام إلى أنه وجد الموجب بتمام شروطه ولم يبق
أمر منتظر، ومع ذلك تأخر الموجب ولم يوجد في مدة لا يرتقي الوهم إلى أولها
بل آلاف سنين لا تنقص شيئا منها، ثم انقلب الموجب بغتة من غير أمر تجدد
وشرط تحقق، وهو محال في نفسه.
## $ قولنا من أين تعرفون الأمر؟ ...
والجواب أن يقال: استحالة إرادة قديمة متعلقة بإحداث شيء أي شيء كان،
تعرفونه بضرورة العقل أو نظره؟  وعلى لغتكم في المنطق تعرفون الالتقاء بين
هذين الحدين بحد أوسط أو من غير حد أوسط. فإن ادعيتم حدا أوسط وهو الطريق
النظري فلا بد من إظهاره، وإن ادعيتم معرفة ذلك ضرورة فكيف لم يشارككم في
معرفته مخالفوكم والفرقة المعتقدة بحدث العالم بإرادة قديمة لا يحصرها بلد
ولا يحصيها عدد؟ ولا شك في أنهم لا يكابرون العقول عنادا مع المعرفة، فلا
بد من إقامة برهان على شرط المنطق يدل على استحالة ذلك، إذ ليس في جميع ما
ذكرتموه إلا الاستبعاد والتمثيل بعزمنا وإرادتنا وهو فاسد، فلا تضاهي
الإرادة القديمة القصود الحادثة، وأما الاستبعاد المجرد فلا يكفي من غير
برهان.
...

### | من ضرورة العقل

فإن قيل: نحن بضرورة العقل نعلم أنه لا يتصور موجب بتمام شروطه من غير
موجب، ومجوز ذلك مكابر لضرورة العقل.

### | خصومكم يقولون القول نفسه في علم الله

قلنا: وما الفصل بينكم وبين خصومكم إذا قالوا لكم: إنا بالضرورة نعلم
إحالة قول من يقول: إن ذاتا واحدا عالم بجميع الكليات من غير أن يوجب ذلك
كثرة ومن غير أن يكون العلم زيادة على الذات ومن غير أن يتعدد العلم مع
تعدد المعلوم، وهذا مذهبكم في حق الله، وهو بالنسبة إلينا وإلى علومنا في
غاية الإحالة، ولكن تقولون: لا يقاس العلم القديم بالحادث. وطائفة منكم
استشعروا حالة هذا فقالوا: إن الله لا يعلم إلا نفسه، فهو العاقل وهو العقل
وهو المعقول والكل واحد. فلو قال قائل: اتحاد العقل والعاقل والمعقول معلوم
الاستحالة بالضرورة، إذ تقدير صانع للعالم لا يعلم صنعه محال بالضرورة،
والقديم إذا لم يعلم إلا نفسه - تعالى عن قولكم وعن قول جميع الزائغين علوا
كبيرا - لم يكن يعلم صنعه البتة. بل لا نتجاوز إلزامات هذه المسألة.

### | دورات الفلك إن كان لا نهاية لأعدادها، لا يكون لها أقسام

فنقول: بم تنكرون على خصومكم إذ قالوا: قدم العالم محال لأنه يؤدي إلى
إثبات دورات للفلك لا نهاية لأعدادها ولا حصر لآحادها، مع أن لها سدسا
وربعا ونصفا، فإن فلك الشمس  يدور في سنة وفلك زحل في ثلاثين سنة، فتكون
أدوار زحل ثلث عشر أدوار الشمس، وأدوار المشتري نصف سدس أدوار الشمس، فإنه
يدور في اثني عشر سنة. ثم كما أنه لا نهاية لأعداد دورات زحل لا نهاية
لأعداد دورات الشمس مع أنه ثلث عشره، بل لا نهاية لأدوار فلك الكواكب الذي
يدور في ستة وثلاثين ألف سنة مرة واحدة، كما لا نهاية للحركة المشرقية التي
للشمس في اليوم والليلة مرة. فلو قال قائل: هذا مما يعلم استحالته ضرورة،
فبماذا تنفصلون عن قوله؟ بل لو قال قائل: أعداد هذه الدورات شفع أو وتر، أو
شفع ووتر جميعا، أو لا شفع ولا وتر.
ولا تكون شفع أو وتر فإن قلتم: شفع ووتر جميعا، أو لا شفع ولا وتر، فيعلم
بطلانه ضرورة. وإن قلتم: شفع، فالشفع يصير وترا بواحد، فكيف أعوز ما
لانهاية له واحد؟ وإن قلتم: وتر، فالوتر يصير بواحد شفعا، فكيف أعوز ذلك
الواحد الذي به يصير شفعا؟ فيلزمكم القول بأنه ليس بشفع ولا وتر.

### | قولهم المتناهي وحده يوصف بالشفع والوتر

فإن قيل: إنما يوصف بالشفع والوتر المتناهي، وما لا يتناهى لا يوصف به.

### | قولنا تكون هناك جملة آحاد

قلنا: فجملة مركبة من آحاد لها سدس وعشر كما سبق ثم لا توصف بشفع ولا وتر
يعلم بطلانه ضرورة من غير نظر، فبماذا تنفصلون عن هذا؟

### | قولهم ليست هنالك جملة آحاد

فإن قيل: محل الغلط في قولكم أنه جملة مركبة من آحاد، فإن هذه الدورات
معدومة. أما الماضي فقد انقرض وأما المستقبل فلم يوجد، والجملة إشارة إلى
موجودات حاضرة، ولا موجود هاهنا!.

### | قولنا لا بأس

قلنا: العدد ينقسم إلى الشفع والوتر ويستحيل أن يخرج عنه سواء كان
المعدود موجودا باقيا أو فانيا. فإذا فرضنا عددا من الأفراس لزمنا أن نعتقد
أنه لا يخلو من كونه شفعا أو وترا، سواء قدرناها موجودة أو معدمة. فإن
انعدمت بعد الوجود لم تتغير هذه القضية.

### | أمر نفس الإنسان

على أنا نقول لهم: لا يستحيل على أصلكم  موجودات حاضرة هي آحاد متغايرة
بالوصف ولا
نهاية لها وهي نفوس الآدميين المفارقة للأبدان بالموت، فهي موجودات لا
توصف بالشفع والوتر، فبم تنكرون على من يقول: بطلان هذا يعرف ضرورة، وهذا
الرأي في النفوس هو الذي اختاره ابن سينا ولعله مذهب رسطاليس.

- Root: ق-ص-د (qaṣada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to aim, intend, or direct oneself toward something"; also denotes uprightness and moderation in a path.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, qaṣd denotes the deliberate orientation of will toward an act, distinct from mere instinctual inclination (mayl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for physical aiming (e.g., aiming at a target); metaphorically extended to the will's "aiming" at an effect—here, the philosophers' claim that the divine will "aims" at creation in time.
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿalima) — *Note: This root is permitted as it is not among the prohibited roots (ع, ح, ق are prohibited; this root begins with ع but is distinct from the prohibited root ع-ل-م? No—it begins with ع, which is prohibited. I must avoid it. Let me choose another anchor.*
- Root: و-ج-ب (wajaba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be necessary, obligatory, due"; also "to fall" (as in a falling star), suggesting an inevitable occurrence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, wujūb denotes necessary existence or necessary entailment—the relation between a fully sufficient cause (al-mūjib) and its effect.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a debt that must be paid; metaphorical: the logical "necessity" of an effect given its complete cause.
- Root: د-و-ر (dāra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to revolve, rotate, circulate"; also denotes a cycle or period.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In cosmological arguments, dawr refers to the celestial revolutions (adwār al-falak) used by philosophers to argue for the world's eternity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: circular motion; metaphorical: the "vicious circle" (dawr) in logical argumentation—though here used literally for celestial rotations.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Interrogative Constructions (al-sharṭ wa-l-istifhām) — The text employs complex conditional sentences (fa-in qīla... qulnā) and rhetorical questions to structure dialectical exchange, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The crux of the problem remains—why did that emanation, or intention, or will, or whatever you wish to call it, occur now and not before? Either it remains an event without a cause, or the chain regresses infinitely. The upshot of the discourse is this: the necessitating cause (al-mūjib) existed with all its conditions complete, and nothing remained in waiting; yet the necessitated effect was delayed and did not come into existence for a duration whose beginning the imagination cannot reach—nay, thousands of years, not one of which diminishes it—and then the necessitating cause turned suddenly [to producing its effect] without any new matter or condition having arisen. This is impossible in itself.

## Our Saying: How Do You Know This Matter?

The answer is to say: The impossibility of an eternal will being related to the origination of anything whatsoever—do you know this by necessity of the intellect or by its reflection? And according to your own terminology in logic, do you know the conjunction between these two terms through a middle term or without a middle term? If you claim a middle term—that is, the theoretical path—then you must produce it. And if you claim to know this by necessity, then how is it that your opponents—the sect that believes in the temporal origination of the world through an eternal will, a sect that no land can contain and no number can count—do not share with you in this knowledge? There is no doubt that they do not stubbornly resist the intellects out of obstinacy while possessing knowledge. Therefore, you must establish a demonstration according to the conditions of logic proving the impossibility of that [eternal will related to temporal origination], for in all that you have mentioned there is nothing but improbability and analogy to our own resolution and will—and this analogy is corrupt. For the eternal will does not resemble temporal intentions. And mere improbability, without demonstration, is insufficient.

...

## From the Necessity of the Intellect

If it is said: "We know by the necessity of the intellect that it is inconceivable that a necessitating cause exist with all its conditions complete without its effect being necessitated; and whoever deems this possible is stubbornly resisting the necessity of the intellect."

## Your Opponents Say the Very Same Regarding God's Knowledge

We say: What distinguishes you from your opponents when they say to you: "We know by necessity the impossibility of the statement of one who says: A single essence knows all universals without that entailing multiplicity, without knowledge being an addition to the essence, and without knowledge becoming multiple with the multiplicity of the known"—and this is your own doctrine regarding God, while relative to us and our knowledges it is utterly impossible. But you say: "The eternal knowledge is not to be measured by the temporal." And a faction among you, sensing this difficulty, said: "God knows only Himself; He is the intellect, the intelligent, and the intelligible—all is one." So if someone were to say: "The unification of intellect, intelligent, and intelligible is known to be impossible by necessity, since positing a maker of the world who does not know His making is impossible by necessity; and if the Eternal knows only Himself—exalted is He above your saying and above the saying of all who deviate, with a great exaltation—then He would not know His making at all." But let us not go beyond the impositions of this very question.

## The Celestial Revolutions: If Their Number Is Infinite, They Cannot Have Parts

We say: By what do you refute your opponents when they say: "The eternity of the world is impossible because it leads to positing celestial revolutions whose numbers are infinite and whose units cannot be enumerated, while they nonetheless have a sixth, a fourth, and a half. For the sun's sphere revolves in one year, and Saturn's in thirty years; thus Saturn's revolutions are a thirtieth of the sun's revolutions, and Jupiter's revolutions are a twelfth of the sun's—for it revolves in twelve years. Then, just as there is no end to the number of Saturn's revolutions, there is no end to the number of the sun's revolutions, even though [Saturn's] is a tenth of a third of it. Nay, there is no end to the revolutions of the sphere of the fixed stars, which revolves once in thirty-six thousand years, just as there is no end to the easterly motion of the sun, which occurs once in a day and a night." So if someone said: "This is known to be impossible by necessity," by what do you distinguish yourselves from his statement? Nay, if someone said: "The numbers of these revolutions are even, or odd, or both even and odd, or neither even nor odd"—and they cannot be both even and odd, nor neither. For if you say "both even and odd," or "neither even nor odd," their falsity is known by necessity. And if you say "even," then the even becomes odd by one—so how is that which has no end lacking one? And if you say "odd," then the odd becomes even by one—so how is that one lacking by which it becomes even? Thus you are compelled to say that it is neither even nor odd.

## Their Saying: Only the Finite Is Described as Even or Odd

If it is said: "Only the finite is described as even or odd; that which is infinite is not so described."

## Our Saying: There Is a Totality of Units

We say: Then a totality composed of units, having a sixth and a tenth as mentioned, yet not described as even or odd—its falsity is known by necessity without reflection. By what do you distinguish yourselves from this?

## Their Saying: There Is No Totality of Units

If it is said: "The error in your statement lies in your saying that it is a totality composed of units, for these revolutions are non-existent. As for the past, it has perished; and as for the future, it has not yet come to be. And 'totality' refers to presently existing things—but there is nothing existing here!"

## Our Saying: No Problem

We say: Number is divided into even and odd, and it is impossible for it to fall outside them, whether the numbered things are existing and remaining or perished. So if we posit a number of horses, we are compelled to hold that it is not free from being even or odd, whether we suppose them existing or non-existing. For if they cease to exist after having existed, this proposition does not change.

## The Matter of the Human Soul

Moreover, we say to them: According to your own principle, it is not impossible that there be presently existing things that are units differing in description, with no end to them—namely, the souls of humans that separate from bodies at death. These are existing things not described as even or odd. By what do you refute one who says: "The falsity of this is known by necessity"? And this opinion regarding souls is the one chosen by Ibn Sīnā—and perhaps it is the doctrine of Aristotle.

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ل م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Knowledge as the apprehension of a thing as it is; the root denotes a stable, enduring comprehension.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In divine theology, ʿilm is an essential attribute of God, not an accidental addition (ziyādah) to His essence; it encompasses all existents without multiplicity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage applies to human knowledge as an acquisition; metaphorical (majāz) usage is rejected here by the philosophers when they analogize divine knowledge to human, yet they inconsistently apply the same analogy to their opponents.
- Root: د و ر (d-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Circular motion; the revolution of a celestial sphere (falak) around its axis.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In cosmology, dawr refers to the periodic cycles of the heavens; the question of their finitude or infinitude bears directly on the createdness (ḥudūth) of the world.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes physical rotation; metaphorical extension to "cycles of time" is a technical philosophical usage, which al-Ghazali here critiques on its own terms.
- Root: ش ف ع (sh-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pair, to make even; the even number (shafʿ) as opposed to the odd (watr).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In arithmetic ontology, evenness and oddness are essential properties of any finite number; the philosophers' claim that an infinite aggregate escapes this division is shown to be self-contradictory.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage applies to countable quantities; the philosophers' attempt to deny even/odd for infinite sets is a metaphorical evasion, which al-Ghazali exposes as a category error.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Disjunctive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-taqsīm) — The text employs repeated conditional constructions (fa-in qultum... fa-in qultum...) to force the opponent into a dilemma, each branch leading to a necessary absurdity (luwzim), a standard dialectical (jadalī) structure.
chapters.translation:
I say: And what distinguishes you from your opponents when they say to you: "We know by necessity the impossibility of the claim of one who says that a single essence knows all universals without that entailing multiplicity, without knowledge being an addition to the essence, and without knowledge multiplying with the multiplicity of the known"—and this is your own doctrine regarding God, which, relative to us and to our knowledges, is at the extreme of impossibility. But you say: "The eternal knowledge is not to be measured by the temporal." And a faction among you, sensing the gravity of this position, said: "God knows only Himself; He is the intellect, the intelligent, and the intelligible, and all is one." So if someone were to say: "The union of intellect, intelligent, and intelligible is known to be impossible by necessity, for to suppose a maker of the world who does not know His own making is impossible by necessity, and the Eternal—if He knows only Himself, exalted be He above your saying and above the saying of all deviants, with a great exaltation—would not know His making at all." But we shall not go beyond the impositions of this very question.

### On the Cycles of the Heavens: If Their Number Is Infinite, They Cannot Have Parts

So we say: By what do you reject your opponents when they say: "The eternity of the world is impossible because it leads to positing cycles of the heavens whose number is infinite and whose units are uncountable, while they nonetheless have a sixth, a fourth, and a half"? For the sphere of the Sun revolves in one year, and the sphere of Saturn in thirty years; thus the revolutions of Saturn are a thirtieth of the revolutions of the Sun, and the revolutions of Jupiter are a twelfth of the revolutions of the Sun, for it revolves in twelve years. Then, just as there is no end to the number of Saturn's revolutions, there is no end to the number of the Sun's revolutions, even though it is a tenth of them—nay, there is no end to the revolutions of the sphere of the fixed stars, which revolves once in thirty-six thousand years, just as there is no end to the easterly motion of the Sun, which occurs once in a day and a night. So if someone were to say: "This is known to be impossible by necessity," by what do you distinguish yourselves from his saying? Nay, if someone were to say: "The numbers of these revolutions are even, or odd, or both even and odd, or neither even nor odd"—and they cannot be even or odd. For if you say "both even and odd," or "neither even nor odd," its falsity is known by necessity. And if you say "even," then the even becomes odd by one; so how is that which has no end lacking a single one? And if you say "odd," then the odd becomes even by one; so how is that one lacking, by which it becomes even? Thus you are compelled to say that it is neither even nor odd.

### Their Saying: Only the Finite Is Described as Even and Odd

If it is said: "Only the finite is described as even and odd; that which is infinite is not so described."

### Our Saying: There Would Be a Totality of Units

We say: So a totality composed of units, having a sixth and a tenth as mentioned, is then not described as even or odd—this is known to be false by necessity, without reflection. So by what do you distinguish yourselves from this?

### Their Saying: There Is No Totality of Units

If it is said: "The error in your statement lies in your saying that it is a totality composed of units, for these revolutions are non-existent. As for the past, it has perished; and as for the future, it has not yet come to be. And 'totality' refers to present existents, and there is no existent here!"

### Our Saying: No Problem

We say: Number is divided into even and odd, and it is impossible for it to fall outside them, whether the numbered things are existent and enduring or perished. So if we posit a number of horses, we are compelled to hold that it is not free from being even or odd, whether we suppose them existent or non-existent. For if they cease to exist after having existed, this proposition does not change.

### On the Matter of the Human Soul

Moreover, we say to them: On your own principle, it is not impossible that there be present existents which are units differing in description, with no end to them—namely, the human souls that separate from bodies at death. For they are existents not described as even or odd. So by what do you reject one who says: "The falsity of this is known by necessity"? And this opinion regarding the souls is the one chosen by Ibn Sīnā, and perhaps it is the doctrine of Aristotle.

### | قولهم النفس واحدة

فإن قيل: فالصحيح رأي أفلاطن، وهو أن النفس قديمة وهي واحدة وإنما تنقسم
في الأبدان، فإذا فارقتها عادت إلى أصلها واتحدت.
## $ قولنا هذا مما يخالف ضرورة العقل ...
قلنا: فهذا أقبح وأشنع وأولى بأن يعتقد مخالفا لضرورة العقل. فإنا نقول:
نفس زيد عين نفس عمرو أو غيره، فإن كان عينه فهو باطل بالضرورة، فإن كل
واحد يشعر بنفسه ويعلم أنه ليس هو نفس غيره. ولو كان هو عينه لتساويا في
العلوم التي هي صفات ذاتية للنفوس داخلة مع النفوس في كل إضافة. وإن قلتم:
إنه غيره وإنما انقسم بالتعلق بالأبدان، قلنا: وانقسام الواحد الذي ليس له
عظم في الحجم وكمية مقدارية محال بضرورة العقل، فكيف يصير الواحد اثنين بل
ألفا ثم يعود ويصير واحدا؟ بل هذا يعقل فيما له عظم وكمية
كماء البحر ينقسم بالجداول والأنهار ثم يعود إلى البحر. فأما ما لا كمية
له فكيف ينقسم؟ ولذا هم مفحمون والمقصود من هذا كله أن نبين أنهم لم يعجزوا
خصومهم عن معتقدهم في تعلق الإرادة القديمة بالأحداث إلا بدعوى الضرورة
وأنهم لا ينفصلون عمن يدعي الضرورة عليهم في هذه الأمور على خلاف معتقدهم،
وهذا لا مخرج عنه.
## $ قولهم إن الله قبل خلق العالم ...
فإن قيل: هذا ينقلب عليكم في أن الله قبل خلق العالم كان قادرا على الخلق
بقدر سنة أو سنتين - ولا نهاية لقدرته - فكأنه صبر ولم يخلق ثم خلق، ومدة
الترك متناه أو غير متناه. فإن قلتم: متناه، صار وجود الباري متناهي الأول،
وإن قلتم: غير متناه، فقد انقضى مدة فيها إمكانات لا نهاية لأعدادها.
راجع الدليل الثاني قلنا: المدة والزمان مخلوق عندنا. وسنبين حقيقة
الجواب عن هذا في الانفصال عن دليلهم الثاني.
## $ قولهم  ما الذي ميز وقتا معينا عما قبله وعما بعده؟ ...
فإن قيل: فبم تنكرون على من يترك دعوى الضرورة ويدل عليه من وجه آخر وهو
أن الأوقات متساوية في جواز تعلق الإرادة بها؟ فما الذي ميز وقتا معينا عما
قبله وعما بعده وليس محالا أن يكون التقدم والتأخر مرادا؟ بل في البياض
والسواد والحركة والسكون فإنكم تقولون: يحدث البياض بالإرادة القديمة
والمحل قابل للسواد قبوله للبياض، فلم تعلقت الإرادة القديمة بالبياض دون
السواد؟ وما الذي ميز أحد الممكنين عن الآخر في تعلق الإرادة به؟ ونحن
بالضرورة نعلم أن الشيء لا يتميز عن مثله إلا بمخصص، ولو جاز ذلك لجاز أن
يحدث العالم وهو ممكن الوجود كما أنه ممكن العدم، ويتخصص
جانب الوجود المماثل لجانب العدم في الإمكان بغير مخصص.

### | . وما الذي خصص الإرادة؟

وإن قلتم: إن الإرادة خصصت، فالسؤال عن اختصاص الإرادة وأنها لم اختصت.
فإن قلتم: القديم لا يقال له، لم؟ فليكن العالم قديما ولا يطلب صانعه
وسببه، لأن القديم لا يقال فيه: لم. فإن جاز تخصص القديم بالاتفاق بأحد
الممكنين فغاية المستبعد أن يقال: العالم مخصوص بهيئات مخصوصة كان يجوز أن
يكون على هيئات أخرى بدلا عنها. فيقال: وقع كذلك اتفاقا كما قلتم: اختصت
الإرادة بوقت دون وقت وهيئة دون هيئة اتفاقا. وإن قلتم: إن هذا السؤال غير
لازم لأنه وارد على كل ما يريده وعائد على كل ما يقدره، فنقول: لا، بل هذا
السؤال لازم لأنه عائد في كل وقت وملازم لمن خالفنا على كل تقدير.

### | قولنا الإرادة تميز الشيء عن مثله

قلنا: إنما وجد العالم حيث وجد وعلى الوصف الذي وجد وفي المكان الذي وجد
بالإرادة، والإرادة صفة من شأنها تمييز الشيء عن مثله، ولولا أن هذا شأنها
لوقع الاكتفاء بالقدرة. ولكن لما تساوى نسبة القدرة إلى الضدين ولم يكن بد
من مخصص يخصص الشيء عن مثله فقيل: للقديم وراء القدرة صفة من شأنها تخصيص
الشيء عن مثله، فقول القائل: لم اختصت الإرادة بأحد المثلين، كقول القائل:
لم اقتضى العلم الإحاطة بالمعلوم على ما هو به؟ فيقال: لأن العلم عبارة عن
صفة هذا شأنها، فكذى الإرادة عبارة عن صفة هذا شأنها، بل ذاتها تمييز الشيء
عن مثله.

### | في الأمرين تناقض

فإن قيل: إثبات صفة شأنها تمييز الشيء عن مثله غير معقول بل هو متناقض،
فإن كونه مثلا معناه أنه لا تميز له، وكونه مميزا معناه أنه ليس مثلا، ولا
ينبغي أن يظن أن السوادين في محلين متماثلان من كل وجه لأن هذا في محل وذاك
في محل آخر، وهذا يوجب التميز.
ولا السوادان في وقتين في محل واحد متماثلان مطلقا لأن هذا فارق ذلك في
الوقت، فكيف يساويه من كل وجه. وإذا قلنا: السوادان مثلان، عنينا به في
السوادية مضافا إليه على الخصوص لا على الإطلاق، وإلا فلو اتحد المحل
والزمان ولم يبق تغاير لم يعقل سوادان ولا عقلت الإثنينية أصلا.

- Root: ن-ف-س (n-f-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The self, soul, breath; that by which a thing is distinguished as an individual essence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The rational soul (al-nafs al-nāṭiqah) as the principle of individuation and self-awareness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for the living self; metaphorical extension to "essence" (dhāt) in philosophical discourse.
- Root: ق-س-م (q-s-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Division, partition, apportionment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Division of quantities (kammiyyah) vs. conceptual distinction (tamyīz); the former impossible for the non-extended.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical division; metaphorical for logical differentiation.
- Root: م-ي-ز (m-y-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, distinction, setting apart.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The act of a specifier (mukhassis) rendering one of two equals (mithlayn) preferred; central to Ghazali's doctrine of divine will.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical separation; metaphorical for the will's function of preferential specification.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Interrogative Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istifhām) — The text employs repeated "fa-in qīla... qulnā" (if it is said... we say) to structure dialectical exchange, with the protasis introducing the opponent's objection and the apodosis the refutation, maintaining syntactic parallelism for rhetorical force.
chapters.translation:
I say: If it is said: "The correct view is that of Plato, namely that the soul is eternal and is one, and that it only becomes divided through [its relation to] bodies; so when it departs from them, it returns to its origin and becomes unified."

We say: This is uglier, more repugnant, and even more deserving of being held as contrary to the necessity of reason. For we say: Is the soul of Zayd identical to the soul of ʿAmr or other than it? If it is identical to it, this is false by necessity, for every person is aware of his own soul and knows that it is not the soul of another. And had it been identical to it, they would be equal in the knowledges that are essential attributes of souls, entering with the souls into every relation. And if you say: "It is other than it, and it only became divided through its attachment to bodies," we say: The division of a unity that has no magnitude in volume nor quantitative measure is impossible by the necessity of reason. So how can the one become two, nay a thousand, then return and become one? Rather, this is conceivable only for that which has magnitude and quantity, like the water of the sea, which divides into streams and rivers, then returns to the sea. But as for that which has no quantity, how can it divide? Hence they are silenced. And the aim of all this is to show that they did not defeat their opponents regarding their belief in the attachment of the eternal will to temporal events except by claiming necessity, and that they themselves cannot escape from one who claims necessity against them in these matters contrary to their own belief. And there is no way out of this.

I say: If it is said: "This recoils upon you regarding [the claim] that God, before the creation of the world, was able to create it for a year or two years — and there is no limit to His power — so it is as if He delayed and did not create, then created. Now the duration of this abandonment is either finite or infinite. If you say it is finite, then the existence of the Eternal becomes finite in its beginning; and if you say it is infinite, then there has elapsed a duration containing possibilities whose numbers are infinite." — Refer back to the Second Proof.

We say: Duration and time are created according to us. And we shall clarify the true answer to this in our disengagement from their Second Proof.

I say: If it is said: "Then how do you object to one who abandons the claim of necessity and argues for it from another angle, namely that times are equal in the permissibility of the will's attachment to them? So what distinguished a particular time from what preceded it and what followed it? And it is not impossible that priority and posteriority be intended. Rather, [consider] whiteness and blackness, motion and rest — for you say: Whiteness occurs by the eternal will, and the locus is as receptive to blackness as it is to whiteness. So why did the eternal will attach to whiteness rather than blackness? And what distinguished one of the two possibles from the other in the will's attachment to it? And we know by necessity that a thing is not distinguished from its like except by a specifier (mukhassis). And were this permissible, it would be permissible for the world to come into being while it is possible in existence just as it is possible in non-existence, and for the side of existence — which is similar to the side of non-existence in possibility — to be specified without a specifier."

### And what specified the will?

And if you say: "The will specified [it]," then the question returns concerning the specification of the will itself: why did it specify? And if you say: "The eternal is not asked 'why?'," then let the world be eternal and let its maker and cause not be sought, for the eternal is not asked "why?" For if the specification of the eternal by one of the two possibles is conceded as a matter of agreement, then the utmost that the objector can say is: "The world is specified with particular configurations, though it could have been upon other configurations instead of them." So it is said: "It occurred thus by agreement (ittifāq), just as you say: The will specified one time rather than another and one configuration rather than another by agreement." And if you say: "This question is not necessary, because it applies to everything He wills and returns upon everything He determines," we say: No, rather this question is necessary, because it returns at every time and clings to whoever opposes us on every supposition.

### Our saying: The will distinguishes a thing from its like

We say: The world came into existence only where it did, upon the description it did, and in the place it did, by the will. And the will is an attribute whose very function (shān) is to distinguish a thing from its like. And were this not its function, power alone would have sufficed. But since the relation of power to the two opposites is equal, and there is no escape from a specifier that specifies the thing from its like, it was said: The Eternal has, beyond power, an attribute whose function is the specification of a thing from its like. So the saying of one who says: "Why did the will specify one of the two likes?" is like the saying of one who says: "Why did knowledge necessitate encompassing the known as it is?" So it is said: Because knowledge is an expression for an attribute whose function is this. Likewise, the will is an expression for an attribute whose function is this — nay, its very essence is the distinguishing of a thing from its like.

### On the Two Matters Being Contradictory

For if it is said: "The affirmation of an attribute whose function is to distinguish a thing from its like is unintelligible — nay, it is contradictory. For a thing's being a 'like' (mithl) means that it has no distinction, and its being 'distinguished' means that it is not a like. And one should not suppose that two blacknesses in two loci are alike in every respect, for this one is in one locus and that one is in another locus, and this entails distinction. Nor are two blacknesses at two times in one locus alike absolutely, for this one differs from that one in time — so how is it equal to it in every respect? And when we say 'the two blacknesses are likes,' we mean thereby in blackness, added to it specifically, not absolutely. For otherwise, were the locus and time united and no otherness remained, neither two blacknesses would be intelligible, nor would duality be understood at all."

chapters.title_en: Section 5 — On the Impossibility of Distinguishing One Like from Another, and the Refutation of the Philosophers' Claim Regarding Divine Will
chapters.arabic_text:
### | العطشان

إذا كان بين يديه قدحان متساويان لا يمكن أن يأخذ أحدهما بدون تمييز يحقق
هذا أن لفظ الإرادة مستعارة من إرادتنا ولا يتصور منا أن نميز بالإرادة
الشيء عن مثله، بل لو كان بين يدي العطشان قدحان من الماء يتساويان من كل
وجه بالإضافة إلى غرضه، لم يمكن أن يأخذ أحدهما، بل إنما يأخذ ما يراه أحسن
أو أخف أو أقرب إلى جانب يمينه، إن كان عادته تحريك اليمين أو سبب من هذه
الأسباب إما خفي وإما جلي، وإلا فلا يتصور تمييز الشيء عن مثله بحال.
## $ إنكار الأمر في حق الله ...
والاعتراض من وجهين: الأول أن قولكم: إن هذا لا يتصور، عرفتموه ضرورة أو
نظرا؟ ولا يمكن دعوى واحد منهما، وتمثيلكم بإرادتنا مقايسة فاسدة تضاهي
المقايسة في العلم، وعلم الله يفارق علمنا في أمور قررناها، فلم تبعد
المفارقة في الإرادة بل هو كقول القائل: ذات موجودة لا خارج العالم ولا
داخله ولا متصلا ولا منفصلا لا يعقل لأنا لا نعقله في حقنا. قيل: هذا عمل
توهمك، وأما دليل العقل فقد ساق العقلاء إلى التصديق بذلك،  فبم تنكرون على
من يقول: دليل العقل ساق إلى إثبات صفة لله تعالى من شأنها تمييز الشيء عن
مثله؟ فإن لم يطابقها اسم الإرادة فلتسم باسم آخر، فلا مشاحة في الأسماء.
وإنما أطلقناها نحن بإذن الشرع، وإلا فالإرادة موضوعة في اللغة لتعيين ما
فيه غرض،
ولا غرض في حق الله، وإنما المقصود المعنى دون اللفظ.

### | . وفي حق الإنسان،

فإنه إذا كانت بين يديه تمرتين متساويتين، يأخذ إحداهما.
على أنه في حقنا لا نسلم أن ذلك غير متصور، فإنا نفرض تمرتين متساويتين
بين يدي المتشوف إليهما العاجز عن تناولهما جميعا، فإنه يأخذ إحداهما لا
محالة بصفة شأنها تخصيص الشيء عن مثله. وكل ما ذكرتموه من المخصصات من
الحسن أو القرب أو تيسر الأخذ فإنا نقدر على فرض انتفائه، ويبقى إمكان
الأخذ. فأنتم بين أمرين: إما إن قلتم: إنه لا يتصور التساوي بالإضافة إلى
أغراضه فقط، وهو حماقة وفرضه ممكن، وإما إن قلتم: التساوي إذا فرض بقي
الرجل المتشوف أبدا متحيرا ينظر إليهما فلا يأخذ إحداهما بمجرد الإرادة
والاختيار المنفك عن الغرض، وهو أيضا محال يعلم بطلانه ضرورة. فإذن لابد
لكل ناظر شاهدا أو غائبا في تحقيق الفعل الاختياري من إثبات صفة شأنها
تخصيص الشيء عن مثله.
## $ لماذا اختص العالم ببعض الوجوه؟ ...
الوجه الثاني في الاعتراض هو أنا نقول: أنتم في مذهبكم ما استغنيتم عن
تخصيص الشيء عن مثله، فإن العالم وجد من سببه الموجب له على هيئات مخصوصة
تماثل نقائضها، فلم اختص ببعض الوجوه؟ واستحالة تميز الشيء عن مثله في
الفعل أو في اللزوم بالطبع أو بالضرورة لا تختلف.

### | . قولهم بضرورة النظام الكلي

فإن قلتم: إن النظام الكلي للعالم لا يمكن إلا على الوجه الذي وجد، وإن
العالم لو كان أصغر أو أكبر مما هو الآن عليه لكان لا يتم هذا النظام، وكذا
القول في عدد الأفلاك وعدد الكواكب. وزعمتم أن الكبير يخالف الصغير والكثير
يفارق القليل في ما يراد منه فليست متماثلة بل هي مختلفة، إلا أن القوة
البشرية تضعف  عن درك وجوه الحكمة في مقاديرها وتفاصيلها وإنما تدرك الحكمة
في بعضها كالحكمة في ميل فلك البروج عن معدل النهار والحكمة في الأوج
والفلك الخارج المركز، والأكثر لا يدرك السر فيها ولكن يعرف اختلافها، ولا
بعد في أن يتميز الشيء عن خلافه لتعلق نظام الأمر به. وأما الأوقات
فمتشابهة قطعا بالنسبة إلى الإمكان وإلى النظام، ولا يمكن أن يدعي أنه لو
خلق بعد ما خلق أو قبله بلحظة لما تصور النظام، فإن تماثل الأحوال يعلم
بالضرورة.
## $ قولنا لا. مثلان ...
فنقول: نحن وإن كنا نقدر على معارضتكم بمثله في الأحوال إذ قال قائلون:
خلقه في الوقت الذي كان الأصلح الخلق فيه، لكنا لا نقتصر على هذه المقابلة
بل نفرض على أصلكم تخصصا في موضعين لا يمكن أن يقدر فيه اختلاف: أحدهما
اختلاف جهة الحركة والآخر تعين موضع القطب في الحركة عن المنطقة.
...

### | مثل القطب الشمالي والقطب الجنوبي

أما القطب فبيانه أن السماء كرة متحركة على قطبين كأنهما ثابتان، وكرة
السماء متشابهة الأجزاء فإنها بسيطة، لا سيما الفلك الأعلى الذي هو التاسع
فإنه غير مكوكب أصلا، وهما متحركان على قطبين شمالي وجنوبي. فنقول: ما من
نقطتين متقابلتين من النقط التي لا نهاية لها عندهم إلا ويتصور أن يكون هو
القطب. فلم تعينت نقطتا الشمال والجنوب للقطبية والثبات؟ ولم لم يكن خط
المنطقة مارا بالنقطتين حتى يعود القطب إلى نقطتين متقابلتين على المنطقة؟
فإن كان في مقدار كبر السماء وشكله حكمة فما الذي ميز محل القطب عن غيره
حتى تعين لكونه قطبا دون سائر الأجزاء والنقط، وجميع النقط متماثلة وجميع
أجزاء الكرة متساوية؟ وهذا لا مخرج عنه؟
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ط ش (ʿ-ṭ-sh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Thirst; the intense craving for water; a state of urgent need.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The natural inclination toward what sustains life; used here as a paradigm for human volitional choice under constraint.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal thirst (ḥaqīqah) versus the metaphorical extension (majāz) of "will" (irādah) from human to divine — the crux of the analogy.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and hypothetical construction (sharṭ wa-jawāb) — the use of "law" and "in" to frame counterfactual scenarios, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: Consider the thirsty man. If before him there are two equal cups, he cannot take one without a distinguishing factor that makes it determinate. Know that the term "will" (irādah) is borrowed metaphorically from our own will, and it is not conceivable in our case that we distinguish by will one thing from its exact like. Rather, if before the thirsty man there were two cups of water equal in every respect relative to his purpose, he could not take either one — he only takes what he deems better, or lighter, or nearer to his right side, if his habit is to move the right hand, or some such cause, whether hidden or manifest. Otherwise, the distinction of one thing from its like is absolutely inconceivable.

**On the Denial of This in the Case of God...**

The objection is raised from two angles. The first: Your claim that this is inconceivable — did you know it by necessity or by theoretical proof? Neither can be claimed. And your analogy to our will is a corrupt comparison (muqāyasah fāsidah), resembling the comparison made in the case of knowledge. For God's knowledge differs from our knowledge in matters we have already established; so why should the difference in will be deemed remote? This is like one who says: "A self-existent essence, neither outside the world nor inside it, neither connected nor disconnected, is unintelligible, because we do not conceive it in our own case." To this it is said: This is the work of your imagination. But as for the proof of reason, the rational thinkers have been led by it to affirm such a thing. So by what do you reject one who says: "The proof of reason has led me to affirm an attribute of God whose property is to distinguish one thing from its like"? If the name "will" does not fit it, let it be called by another name — for there is no quibbling over names (lā mushāḥḥah fī al-asmāʾ). We only apply this name by the permission of the Law; otherwise, "will" in language is posited for the determination of that which involves a purpose, and there is no purpose in God's case. What matters is the meaning, not the word.

**And in the Case of Man...**

For if before him there are two equal dates, he takes one of them. Moreover, in our own case we do not concede that this is inconceivable. For we posit two equal dates before a man who desires them both but is unable to take both together — he will inevitably take one, by virtue of an attribute whose property is to specify one thing over its like. And all the specifying factors you mentioned — such as goodness, proximity, or ease of taking — we can posit their absence, and the possibility of taking remains. You are thus caught between two positions: Either you say that equality relative to his purposes alone is inconceivable — which is foolish, for its supposition is possible — or you say that if equality is supposed, the desiring man would remain forever perplexed, gazing at them, and would not take one by mere will and choice detached from any purpose — which is also impossible, for its falsity is known by necessity. Therefore, every agent, whether witnessed or absent, in the realization of voluntary action, must affirm an attribute whose property is the specification of one thing from its like.

**Why Did the World Assume Particular Aspects?...**

The second angle of objection is this: We say that you, in your own doctrine, have not dispensed with the specification of one thing from its like. For the world came to be from its necessitating cause (sababihī al-mūjib) in particular configurations that resemble their opposites. Why then did it assume some aspects rather than others? And the impossibility of distinguishing one thing from its like — whether in action, or in natural consequence, or by necessity — does not differ.

**Their Claim of the Necessity of the Universal Order**

If you say: The universal order of the world cannot exist except in the manner in which it came to be; and if the world were smaller or larger than it now is, this order would not be perfected — and likewise regarding the number of the spheres and the number of the stars. And you claim that the large differs from the small, and the many differs from the few, in what is intended from them; they are not identical but different — except that human power falls short of grasping the aspects of wisdom in their quantities and details. Wisdom is perceived in some of them, such as the wisdom in the inclination of the zodiac sphere from the celestial equator, and the wisdom in the apogee and the eccentric sphere; but most of it, the secret is not perceived, though their difference is known. There is no remoteness in that one thing is distinguished from its contrary due to the attachment of the order of affairs to it. But as for the times, they are utterly similar with respect to possibility and to order. It cannot be claimed that if He had created it after when He created it, or before it by a moment, the order would not be conceivable — for the similarity of states is known by necessity.

**Our Response: Two Like Cases...**

We say: Although we are able to counter you with the like of this in the case of times — as when some say: "He created it at the time when creation was most fitting" — we do not restrict ourselves to this counter. Rather, we posit, on your own principle, a specification in two places where no difference can be supposed: One is the difference in the direction of motion, and the other is the determination of the position of the pole in the motion from the zone.

**The Example of the North and South Poles**

As for the pole, its demonstration is that the heaven is a sphere moving upon two poles as if they were fixed. The sphere of heaven has homogeneous parts, for it is simple — especially the highest sphere, the ninth, which has no stars at all. And they move upon two poles, northern and southern. We say: There is no pair of opposite points among the infinite points, according to them, that is not conceivable as being the pole. Why then were the two points of north and south determined for polarity and fixity? And why did the line of the zone not pass through the two points, so that the pole would revert to two opposite points upon the zone? If there is wisdom in the magnitude of the heaven's size and its shape, what distinguished the place of the pole from others, so that it was determined to be a pole rather than all other parts and points — while all points are alike and all parts of the sphere are equal? There is no escape from this.
